title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory audit (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) that tested conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact‑match, fuzzy 5‑gram shingle, and provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy on a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample using a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) and a deterministic NetOps validator. Key outcomes (artifact‑verified): no high‑confidence contamination flags were produced; baseline = 150/150 validator passes, guarded = 150/150 validator passes; paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Critically, the executed confirmatory sample consisted of provenance‑stable synthetic tasks produced by a deterministic task generator (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). Those two facts—explicitly permitted by the preregistration—produced identical model outputs for baseline and guarded conditions when no high‑confidence flags occurred and therefore made the paired test degenerate for detecting generation‑level contamination effects in this run. The archived execution and analysis artifacts (task_manifest, transformation_manifest, deterministic_reconciliation, analysis artifacts) fully substantiate these facts; the contamination detector logs contain no recorded overlap scores requiring deterministic replacements, so per‑item fuzzy‑overlap summary statistics are absent from the archive and cannot be reported here. We reconcile preregistration→execution, explain why the null is artifact‑grounded, and provide concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (provenance‑rich public sampling, independent regeneration, multi‑model scope, paraphrase‑robust detectors, and matched power calculations) to increase audit sensitivity in future work.

sections.introduction: LLM-driven NetOps tools are proposed to translate operator intent into concrete device configurations and to propose automated repairs. Reliable empirical evaluation of such systems requires contamination-aware protocols: if benchmark items (or templated tasks) are present in a model's training corpus, measured accuracy can be inflated and operational risk underestimated. We preregistered a focused confirmatory audit to operationalize conservative, deterministic contamination detectors and a guarded exclusion policy, then measure whether applying those controls changes validator‑based success rates in a reproducible sample. Research question (preregistered): after freezing deterministic contamination‑detection and treatment rules, how many high‑confidence contamination flags occur in a reproducible 150‑item sample, and how much does applying those controls change an LLM's validator pass rate? Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, archived paired confirmatory experiment executed under the frozen plan; (2) artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 with deterministic validator traces; (3) a preregistration→execution reconciliation that identifies mechanistic causes of a degenerate null and prescribes stronger future audit designs. Important execution facts (stated up front): the confirmatory sample used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (deterministic task generator) and execution adopted shared_initial_candidate semantics such that, absent high‑confidence exclusions, a single generation per item was reused for both baseline and guarded episodes. These execution facts are archived (task_manifest.jsonl, model_configuration.json, deterministic_reconciliation) and materially limit this run's sensitivity to detect generation‑level contamination effects; we make this limitation explicit here and in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.related_work: Prior NetOps and LLM literature shows encouraging capability for intent→configuration synthesis and for generate–validate–repair patterns that improve average reliability versus naive generation. Systems and benchmarks (recent work) demonstrate that integrating validators and iterative repair reduces regressions, but results vary by dataset construction, model family, and task realism. Formal and deterministic verification tools (header‑space analysis and related systems) are established oracles for reachability/policy checks and are commonly used as validators in produce–validate workflows. Separately, methodological surveys of LLM evaluation highlight contamination and construct‑validity risks: web‑crawled corpora can contain near‑identical or templated items that leak into model training data, and naive benchmark protocols without provenance tracing or n‑gram overlap checks are vulnerable to inflated accuracy. Those critiques directly motivated our preregistered detectors (exact canonical equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance timestamp heuristics) and the guarded deterministic replacement policy used in the audit. Where this study differs: we preregistered conservative detectors and an explicit guarded treatment, archived all deterministic execution traces and validators, and report exact artifact‑grounded reconciliation when the execution produced a degenerate paired outcome.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimands. The study preregistration (contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) defined the primary estimand as the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) across item×model pairs, tested with an exact McNemar two‑sided test. Confirmatory sample: 150 item pairs (planned_episode_count = 300 episodes). A paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI used 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Contamination detectors and guarded treatment. The preregistered detectors were: (1) exact normalized token equality after canonicalization; (2) 5‑gram shingle fuzzy overlap with preregistered thresholds (high‑confidence flag if overlap ≥ 0.80; medium if 0.50–0.80); and (3) provenance heuristics comparing item timestamps to model cutoff. The guarded rule deterministically excluded high‑confidence‑flagged items and replaced them using deterministic retemplating/topology augmentation sampled from the same generator distribution with fixed seeds; replacement acceptance required intent‑preserving embedding similarity. Validator and executor. The verification oracle was a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) that returns deterministic pass/fail outcomes based on required final state and workflow policies; analysis used the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor. Sampling and generation semantics (critical). The preregistration permitted deterministic generators and deterministic replacements when necessary. The executed run used a deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) that produced provenance‑stable synthetic items (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for the confirmatory sample. Execution settings set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate): a single shared generation was produced per item and reused for both baseline and guarded episodes when no high‑confidence exclusions occurred. Because no high‑confidence flags were produced, the shared generation semantics reduced actual model calls to one per item (model_calls_used = 150) rather than two. The deterministic_reconciliation artifact documents these settings and the pair accounting. Planned sensitivity and prespecified analyses. The preregistration included two prespecified sensitivity analyses: treating failed model calls as failures and fuzzy‑threshold sensitivity at 0.50/0.65/0.80. Power guidance in the preregistration showed the single‑model design has reduced sensitivity versus a multi‑model design and that detectable paired differences depend on baseline rate and within‑pair correlation; these planning curves are archived in the preregistration artifacts.

The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags for the executed sample; the archived contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged episodes. Because no high‑confidence flags were produced, the guarded policy performed no deterministic replacements and the transformation_manifest shows no replacement entries. sections.discussion: Why the degenerate null occurred. The degenerate null (perfect agreement) is artifact‑grounded and arises from two execution facts present in the archive: (1) the sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic tasks from a deterministic task generator (source_identifier "synthetic-netops:"), and (2) shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) produced a single shared generation per item that, in the absence of high‑confidence flags, was reused for both baseline and guarded episodes. Both facts were permitted by the preregistration and are recorded in the archived task_manifest, transformation_manifest, and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts; no deviations_from_preregistration were logged. What this run answers (and does not). This execution answers the preregistered question in the concrete sampling regime used: given provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and conservative detectors, do high‑confidence flags arise and do guarded exclusions change validator pass rates? For this synthetic sample and generation semantics, the answer is: no high‑confidence flags, and no change in validator pass rate. The result does not generalize to web‑sourced public benchmarks, to paraphrase‑level contamination, to independent regeneration semantics, or to other models. Design lessons (artifact‑anchored recommendations). The archived execution suggests practical audit improvements directly supported by preregistration and execution artifacts: (1) sample provenance‑rich public items (avoid exclusively deterministic synthetic generators when the audit objective is contamination detection); (2) set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded generations are independent per item; (3) expand scope to multiple models and independent seeds to increase observable discordance; (4) layer paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication for borderline flags (the preregistration prespecified fuzzy thresholds but the detector logs here produced no thresholded flags); (5) align sample size to a targeted minimal detectable paired effect using formal power calculations matched to the final multi‑model design. Each recommendation is directly traceable to the preregistration text and to execution artifacts (preregistration plan, transformation_manifest, deterministic_reconciliation, analysis_log).
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation. In the reproducible 150‑pair synthetic sample we observed zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). The degenerate null is artifact‑supported and stems from provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics; it does not imply absence of contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks. We provide explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation, confirm that deterministic reconciliation checks passed, and recommend concrete, artifact‑supported design changes (provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation, multi‑model scope, paraphrase‑sensitive detectors, and matched power calculations) to increase audit sensitivity in future work. All generation prompts, model outputs, validator traces, sampling seeds, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived as part of the execution bundle for independent verification.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or proprietary training corpora.

Sampled items for this run were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:"); the absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in web‑sourced public benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thereby limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds). Subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication.

Passing the deterministic NetOps validator indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
